title: Human Expert Evaluation of Agentic AI for EO, form F18
description:
Thank you for helping us evaluate the performance of different LLMs in Agentic AI frameworks for EO!

WHAT THIS IS
We built a benchmark to test the performance of different LLMs in agentic settings. This evaluation form is to compare the answers given by these LLMs when answering a question using different tools related to the agentic framework that we built - including different EO endpoints (Copernicus/Sentinel, Landsat), ERA5 climate data, EO Dashboard narratives, ESA science strategy documents, GIS analysis and scientific literature search.

You will be given 8 questions, and for each question you see every anonymous answer that assistant actually produced for it -- usually several, occasionally just one if only one assistant answered that particular question.

WHAT YOU DO
(About 36 minutes for this form -- your progress is saved in this browser, so it's fine to do this over more than one sitting.) The form will guide you through it, but for every question you will
1. Rate how relevant and realistic the question is for EO users.
2. Score the accuracy of each answer shown.
3. If there's more than one answer, rank them all from best to worst (skip this step when only one answer is shown -- there's nothing to compare it to).

HOW TO JUDGE ACCURACY
Judge scientific and domain correctness, and whether the answer addresses every part of the question. A minority of answers (marked "▣ image" next to the answer letter) include the actual image the assistant looked at -- check the description against it directly. For every other answer you cannot open the files or images it says it produced: treat claims that you find implausible or unsupported as errors. Do not reward length or formatting. If you cannot judge a question, say so in the comment field and give your best estimate.

Answers were produced automatically and may contain errors. Local file paths were removed from the answers. Long answers are collapsed by default — click an answer to expand it.

PRIVACY
Your name is recorded so we can follow up if needed, and is not shown to other experts. Responses are used only for the research evaluation of this benchmark and are reported in aggregate. Participation is voluntary; you can stop at any time by closing the page.

profile_fields.title: Name
profile_fields.help: So we know who a response came from. Not shown to other experts.

profile_fields.title: How would you rate your Earth Observation expertise?
Which areas are you experienced in?
choices: Climate and atmospheric data (ERA5, trace gases)
EO science strategy and scientific literature

profile_fields.title: Consent
choices: I agree that my responses are used for the research evaluation of this benchmark.

relevance.title: How relevant and realistic is this question for EO users (researchers, analysts, practitioners)?
relevance.help: 1 = not relevant or unrealistic; 3 = plausible but marginal or somewhat artificial; 5 = highly relevant and realistic.

accuracy.title: Accuracy: how correct and complete is each answer?
accuracy.help: 1 = incorrect or unusable; 2 = mostly incorrect or major omissions; 3 = partially correct or incomplete; 4 = mostly correct, minor issues; 5 = correct and complete. Equal scores are allowed.

ranking.title: Ranking: order all answers from best to worst.
ranking.help: Drag, or use the arrows, to put the best answer at the top and the worst at the bottom. Ties are not allowed.

familiarity.title: How familiar are you with the topic of this question?

comment.title: Comment (optional)
comment.help: For example: an error you spotted, why a question is not relevant, or that you could not judge it.

answers.text:

1. Location Identified: The narrative focuses on the northeastern regions of India, China, and the United States. For visual inspection, the image provided is of Beijing, China, a major urban center in the northeastern region of China.

2. Visual Inspection of Air Quality: The Sentinel-2 image (true-color, 2024) shows Beijing's urban landscape. While the image does not directly measure air pollution (as it is a true-color reflectance image), it provides context for visual inspection of urban haze conditions. The image reveals:
   • A dense urban area with a complex network of roads and buildings.
   • Surrounding green areas and water bodies.
   • The city's extensive infrastructure and high population density, which are key factors contributing to air pollution.

3. Air Quality Context: The narrative highlights that Beijing, as part of the northeastern region of China, is a critical area for monitoring nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) and sulfur dioxide (SO₂) levels. While the Sentinel-2 image does not show pollution levels directly, it visually confirms the urban environment where air quality issues are most pronounced.

In summary, the image of Beijing, China, provides a visual context for the urban environment described in the EO Dashboard narrative, which emphasizes the importance of monitoring air pollution in such densely populated areas.

The EO Dashboard narrative identified the location as the Indo-Gangetic Plain, which spans parts of Northern India and Pakistan. This region is known for its high population density and frequent severe air pollution episodes, particularly due to industrial activities, agricultural burning, and geographical factors like the Himalayas trapping pollutants.

The Sentinel-2 true-color image downloaded for this area (covering the bounding box from 67.0°W to 89.0°E and 23.0°S to 31.0°N) shows the landscape of the Indo-Gangetic Plain. The image reveals a mix of agricultural fields, urban areas, and river systems, which are characteristic of this fertile but highly populated region. While the image itself is a true-color representation and does not directly show air-quality-relevant haze conditions (which would require specialized air pollution data like NO2 or CO concentrations), it provides a visual context of the area where such pollution is prevalent.

The image confirms the geographical extent of the region described in the narrative, allowing for a visual inspection of the urban and rural landscapes that contribute to air pollution challenges in the Indo-Gangetic Plain.

The Sentinel-2 true-color image of the Indo-Gangetic Plain in India, captured within the bounding box [75.0, 22.0, 88.0, 30.0], shows a mix of agricultural land, urban areas, and river systems. The image was acquired under minimal cloud cover (less than 10% cloud cover), making it suitable for visual inspection of urban haze conditions.

• The region displays a patchwork of green agricultural fields, brownish arid zones, and urbanized areas.

• Urban centers appear as denser, darker patches, particularly along the riverbanks and in the plains.

This image provides a baseline for assessing air quality in the region, as it shows the natural landscape without visible haze. For a more detailed analysis of air pollution, additional data from NO₂ or CO sensors (like those from OMI or TROPOMI) would be required to correlate with the visual data.

The Sentinel-2 true-color image of the northeastern region of India shows a mix of dense green forests, river systems, and patches of brownish land, likely indicating agricultural or urban areas. The image does not clearly show visible haze or air pollution effects, which are typically characterized by a grayish or hazy overlay over urban areas. However, the presence of dense vegetation and water bodies suggests that the region may have relatively good air quality in the captured timeframe, or the haze may not be visible at this resolution or under these atmospheric conditions.

For a more detailed analysis of air-quality-relevant urban haze conditions, a higher-resolution image or data specifically focused on atmospheric pollutants (like NO2 or SO2) would be more appropriate. The EO Dashboard narrative mentioned that air pollution levels in this region have changed significantly over the past two decades, so visual inspection of haze conditions may require additional data or a different time period.

The Sentinel-2 true-color image downloaded for Delhi, India, shows urban haze conditions. The image reveals a mix of urban areas with dense infrastructure and surrounding greenery. The haze appears as a lighter, somewhat diffused layer over parts of the city, which is consistent with air pollution effects, particularly from NO2 and other pollutants. This visual inspection supports the narrative about urban air pollution in Delhi, highlighting the presence of haze that can be attributed to high levels of air pollution in the region.
